sysd-q-010.title: Access control lists: a permission list on every resource
sysd-q-010.text: Take a file with a short list attached: Alice may read and write, Bob may only read. That list is an access control list, or ACL. It is a list of permissions attached to a system resource, saying which users or system processes may access it and which operations they may perform. Each entry in a typical ACL names a subject, the user or process asking for access, and an operation. A filesystem ACL is a table of access-control entries giving individual users' or groups' rights to specific objects. On routers, switches and servers, an ACL applies rules to ports or IP addresses, with the hosts or networks allowed to use them, much like a firewall. ACLs are easy to understand but error-prone with a high maintenance cost. Maintaining authorization data often costs as much administration as managing authentication credentials. The minimal form of the model in {{ref:sysd-q-014}} is equivalent to an ACL whose only entries are groups. Modern SQL-based ACLs manage groups and inheritance in a hierarchy, so they can express everything that model expresses.

sysd-q-014.title: Role-based access control: permissions through roles
sysd-q-014.text: When someone joins a company or changes departments, a role-based system needs only one change: assigning the right roles. Role-based access control, or RBAC, restricts system access to authorized users and is defined around roles and privileges rather than individual users. Roles are created for job functions and permissions are assigned to roles, so users get permissions only through their roles. The model has subjects, roles, permissions and sessions, with many-to-many assignments, and a subject may have several simultaneous sessions in different roles. Roles can form a hierarchy in which higher-level roles subsume the permissions of sub-roles, and constraints can enforce the rule explained in {{ref:sysd-q-084}}. RBAC eases administration in large organizations with hundreds of users and thousands of permissions, and Kubernetes offers it, with each role listing allowed actions. The costs are role explosion when finer granularity is needed, and extreme complexity across dozens of systems without hierarchical roles. An ACL grants or denies write access to a particular file, whereas an RBAC permission is an operation, such as creating a credit account in a financial application.

sysd-q-011.title: Discretionary access control: the owner decides
sysd-q-011.text: In discretionary access control, or DAC, whoever holds a permission may hand it on. It restricts access to objects by the identity of subjects or the groups they belong to. It is discretionary because a subject holding a permission can pass it, perhaps indirectly, to any other subject, unless restrained by {{ref:sysd-q-012}}. In the common owner-based implementation, each object has an owner who controls its permissions and can make policy decisions. DAC is built on ACLs, and the owner group's policy grants or restricts access. The Unix file mode is a straightforward example, with read, write and execute bits for User, Group and Others. Capability systems are a second implementation. Subjects can transfer access, but not to just any subject, since the passer must already have access to the receiver, in line with least privilege. DAC is easy and flexible, but permission control is scattered and the object's owner group has too much power.

sysd-q-013.title: Attribute-based access control: rules over attributes
sysd-q-013.text: A user can edit a document if they own it and it is in draft mode. A rule like that, built from attributes, is attribute-based access control, or ABAC, in miniature. ABAC is an access control paradigm in which a subject's authorization is decided by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the requested operation and sometimes the environment. Its policy rules are Boolean functions of those attributes, so the only limits are the policy language and the availability of attributes. The attributes fall into four categories: subject (age, clearance, department, role), action (read, delete, approve), object (type, department, classification, location) and contextual (time, location). Unlike {{ref:sysd-q-014}}, ABAC expresses complex rule sets over many attributes and needs no explicit authorizations for individual subjects. It can protect API methods, such as allowing managers to approve transactions up to their approval limit. The recommended architecture divides the work among the points described in {{ref:sysd-q-085}}. ABAC is flexible, but its rules can be complicated and the implementation hard, and more granular controls add performance overhead.

sysd-q-085.title: Policy decision and enforcement points: who asks, who decides
sysd-q-085.text: In an API, the business logic can run only after another component has said Permit. An interceptor asks a Policy Decision Point (PDP) whether the caller may perform an action. The PDP fetches the policy and attributes and returns Permit or Deny, and only on Permit is the business logic called. That is authorization split into points. Each independent policy must be retrieved, evaluated and enforced. A Policy Retrieval Point retrieves it from a policy repository, the PDP evaluates it, and a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) enforces it. The PEP intercepts a user's request to a resource, asks the PDP whether access is approved or rejected, and acts on the answer. The PDP is the central, environment-independent point that makes the final decision: Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate. Policy Information Points hold the data that policy conditions are evaluated against, such as resource status, session state or time of day. The PDP queries them for attribute values when needed.

sysd-q-082.title: XACML: a policy language, not an engine
sysd-q-082.text: XACML says how to write an access policy, but not how to build the engine that evaluates it. It is an XML-based standard markup language for specifying access control policies, published by OASIS. It defines a declarative, fine-grained, attribute-based policy language, an architecture and a processing model for evaluating access requests, and it can also implement role-based access control. In the architecture of {{ref:sysd-q-085}}, the enforcement point converts the user's request into an XACML authorization request. The decision point evaluates it and returns Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate. When rules contradict each other, combining algorithms such as deny-unless-permit and permit-unless-deny merge their decisions into one. An obligation is a directive from the decision point to the enforcement point on what must happen before or after approval, such as logging. If the enforcement point cannot comply, access may not be realized, while advice may be ignored. Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source decision point. XACML 3.0 added delegation, which lets an authority hand all or part of its authority to another user without modifying the root policy.

sysd-q-086.title: The AAA authorization framework: chained agreements
sysd-q-086.text: In the AAA authorization framework, a request succeeds only if two agreements are both honored: user to home organization, and home organization to service provider. It is a framework for understanding the authorization of Internet resources and services, assuming the parties are already authenticated. It names four entities: the user, the home organization, the provider's AAA server, and the service equipment that delivers the service. There are three sequences. In the agent sequence the AAA server applies policy and configures the equipment. In pull the equipment asks the AAA server. In push the user first gets a ticket from the AAA server and presents it to the equipment.

sysd-q-012.title: Mandatory access control: a policy users cannot override
sysd-q-012.text: In mandatory access control, or MAC, the policy is not the user's to change. A secured environment, such as an operating system or database, constrains a subject's ability to access or modify an object under a centrally set policy. Subjects and objects carry security attributes, which the kernel checks against the policy on every access. Users cannot override the policy or grant access to restricted files, unlike in DAC. Once tied to multilevel security and military systems, MAC now reaches mainstream systems through SELinux, AppArmor and Windows Mandatory Integrity Control. It is strict and straightforward but not flexible.

sysd-q-083.title: Relationship-based access control: permission through relationships
sysd-q-083.text: In a social network, users share posts with other specific users, so who may see a post depends on who is connected to whom. Relationship-based access control, or ReBAC, evolved from RBAC. In it, a subject's permission to access a resource is defined by the presence of relationships between subjects and resources. It allows fine-grained permissions of exactly that kind. ABAC attributes can be compared with one another to give relation-based control, and XACML conditions can implement relationship-based access control.

sysd-q-084.title: Separation of duties: two people for critical operations
sysd-q-084.text: The same person should not both create a login account and authorize its creation. That is separation of duties: two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations, so no individual can breach security through dual privilege. By extension, no person may hold a role that exercises audit, control or review authority over another role held at the same time. In RBAC, constraints that restrict permission inheritance from opposing roles achieve it, and RBAC is particularly well suited to it. XACML conditions can implement segregation-of-duty checks.

sysd-q-009.title: Designing a permission system, from ACLs to policy points
sysd-q-009.text:
The task is to design the part of a system that decides what each user may do. Authorization sits after authentication, which is assumed done. It is itself a security mechanism, so it must not be easy to abuse to get around the protection it provides.

The simplest model is an ACL, covered in {{ref:sysd-q-010}}: a list of rules granting or denying users access to a resource. It is easy to understand, but error-prone with a high maintenance cost. In DAC the owner decides, as {{ref:sysd-q-011}} explains: an access policy set by the object's owner group grants or restricts access. It is easy and flexible, but permission control is scattered and the owner group has too much power. In MAC, covered in {{ref:sysd-q-012}}, a central policy and classification labels on owners and resources decide access, and users cannot override it. It is strict and straightforward but not flexible.

The data model of RBAC, covered in {{ref:sysd-q-014}}, is subjects, roles and permissions with many-to-many assignments. Permissions attach to roles, users acquire them only through roles, and a subject can hold several sessions in different roles. Roles can form a hierarchy in which higher roles subsume permissions of sub-roles. Constraints enforce separation of duties, such as not letting one person both create and authorize an account. RBAC is flexible in assigning roles and accepted as best practice within a single system, but it can suffer role explosion when finer granularity is needed.

ABAC evaluates attributes of the subject, the action, the resource and the environment through Boolean policy rules; {{ref:sysd-q-013}} describes it. It is flexible, but its rules can be complicated and the implementation is hard. Relationship-based control, in {{ref:sysd-q-083}}, defines permission by the relationships between subjects and resources. This gives fine-grained permissions, for example in a social network where users share posts with specific other users. The models combine: RBAC can implement DAC or MAC policies, and ABAC and relationship-based access control build on RBAC.

Whichever model is chosen, the check is split into points, as in {{ref:sysd-q-085}}. A PEP intercepts the request and asks a PDP, which evaluates policies fetched through a retrieval point and gets attributes from information points. In an API, an interceptor asks the PDP whether Alice can approve transaction 123. The PDP retrieves the policy and attributes and returns Permit or Deny, and only Permit runs the business logic; otherwise access is denied. XACML supplies a policy language and request/response scheme, but its specification does not cover how a PDP is built. Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source PDP. When rules contradict, combining algorithms such as deny-unless-permit or permit-unless-deny resolve the conflict into one final decision. An obligation tells the PEP what must happen around an approved access, such as logging; if the PEP cannot comply, the approved access may not be realized.

Fine-grained checks cost performance. The more granular the controls, the higher the overhead. RFC 2904 says the fields for both authentication and authorization should travel in a single message set to reduce latency. To remember: the shape stays the same across models. A request is intercepted, a decision point answers Permit or Deny, and the answer is enforced.

openers.design-a-permission-system: A permission system answers one question: may this subject perform this operation on this resource? Authorization sits after authentication, which is assumed done, and it is itself a security mechanism that must not be easy to abuse to get around the protection it provides. The models in this chapter answer the question in different ways: a list of permissions attached to a resource, roles and privileges, the discretion of an object's owner, the evaluation of attributes, relationships between subjects and resources, or a policy set centrally. Around them sit the points that retrieve, evaluate and enforce a policy, the standards that describe them, and the requirement that two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations.

reviews.design-a-permission-system: The models differ in who holds the power. An ACL lists permissions on each resource, DAC lets the owner pass them on, MAC takes that power away with a central policy, RBAC groups permissions into roles, ABAC evaluates attributes and ReBAC follows relationships. Beneath them, the enforcement, decision and information points split the check, XACML supplies a policy language for it, and the AAA framework chains agreements between organizations. Separation of duties keeps any one person from authorizing a critical operation alone, and the worked design shows these pieces combining, at a cost in performance that grows with granularity.
